## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### New: The Sihanoukville count
*Jul 1966 – Nov 1967 · Sihanoukville (Kompong Som), Route 4 and Kompong Speu, and the roads to the base areas of the Fishhook and the Parrot's Beak, Cambodia; Tan Son Nhut and Washington · EV003-4*

*Initiative: allied*
By the summer of 1966 the sea route that TIDE TABLE had closed had been a year in Cambodia, and the argument over it was the oldest in the intelligence community. Historically MACV J-2 held that most of the arms for the war in III and IV Corps came through Sihanoukville, and the CIA held that the port's traffic was mostly rice and contraband, until the records of the Hak Ly Trucking Company, seized after Lon Nol's coup in 1970, showed about 21,600 tons of arms and ammunition moved through the port between December 1966 and April 1969. Here the argument was settled by counting, in the first half of 1967.

The count had three sources. The U-2S photographed the port obliquely from the Gulf of Siam, from outside Cambodian airspace, about twice a month: ships alongside, their flags, cargo on the quays and trucks in the marshalling area. The Global Hawk, on the nights the orbit could be spared from the coast, stood off over Tay Ninh and Binh Long inside South Vietnamese airspace and watched the road traffic up to 150–200 kilometres into Cambodia: convoys of ten to thirty trucks moving at night from Kompong Speu and Kompong Cham toward Snoul, Mimot and the Fishhook, and toward Svay Rieng and the Parrot's Beak, stopping at depots that did not appear on any Cambodian map¹. And from May 1967 the reconnaissance teams of MACV's Studies and Observations Group, crossing the border under Operation Daniel Boone, were sent to look at the points where the convoys stopped. The radar did not see what the trucks carried. The teams, twice, found ammunition crates with Chinese markings in the depots the tracks had led them to; one team of three Americans and nine Montagnards was lost near Mimot in September 1967².

On 9 March 1967 MACV J-2 and the CIA's Office of Current Intelligence agreed a joint estimate: that between July 1965 and February 1967 about 9,000–13,000 tons of military cargo had moved from Sihanoukville to the border base areas, and that the route supplied most of the arms and ammunition of the PAVN and VC forces in III and IV Corps. Lieutenant Colonel Harold Kessling's cell had built the count night by night for twenty months. The Joint Chiefs proposed in April a naval quarantine of Sihanoukville and air strikes on the depots; the President declined both, and Sihanouk's neutrality, and the bar on operations into Cambodia, stood². The estimate changed no rule. It changed the argument: from 1967 the war's central sanctuary was a measured fact, and the case for and against relief of the Cambodian constraint was made from evidence, three years before history made it from captured ledgers.

## Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

### Overview (changed)

1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals of the South at once, breaking the Tet truce and every assumption of the American progress campaign. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no general uprising, the cities are retaken, Hue after a month, and the Viet Cong lose the larger part of the cadres and local forces they had built over a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes. Within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's request for 206,000 more men, offered negotiations, kept the bombing of the whole North, and withdrawn from the presidential race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592 in the year, the highest of the war, and US strength in Vietnam stands at about 537,000 at its end³.

The phase has three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, and three American responses. The first is military: Khe Sanh is held under the heaviest bombardment in the history of air warfare, the cities are cleared, and a new commander, General Creighton W. Abrams, takes over in June. The second is political: the decision of 31 March caps the American commitment, and in this war, with no partial halt to trade, the talks wait for the full halt in November. The third is the countryside: with the VC's main and local forces weakened and its infrastructure exposed in the offensive, the government and CORDS move into the vacuum, with a general mobilization in June, the Phoenix programme and an Accelerated Pacification Campaign from November. The year ends with the bombing of the North stopped, a new president elected on a promise to end the war, and the war's centre of gravity shifting from the American divisions to the territorial forces and the hamlets.

The human cost in the South is the heaviest of the war to date. The offensive and the counter-attacks create about 630,000 new refugees, on top of about 800,000 displaced before; more than 70,000 homes are destroyed; by the end of the year about one South Vietnamese in twelve lives in a refugee camp. The government counts 14,300 civilian dead and 24,000 wounded in the first phase alone⁴.

In this war the year runs on the same dates and turns the same way. Tet is still decided in Saigon, Hue and Khe Sanh, and in Washington⁵. What changes is the Delta, the hamlets and the army that met the offensive.

In the held belt the Front attacks from a smaller base. It recruits fewer men in the titled districts of the Bassac and the coastal Centre in 1968. The hamlets around the western Delta towns warn the garrisons and do not hide the attackers. The Special Branch knows the Front's urban cadres. Its guides do not arrive. A third of the leaders it sends into the Delta towns to direct the uprising are taken in February, because the district centres had charted them for three years⁵⁶⁷. On the northwestern road to Tan Son Nhut its columns cross Hoc Mon through hamlets that have no resident cadres left to guide them. In Hue its lists are better than elsewhere, because the Republic's own census fed them. The province centre's informant cards burn in the first hour; the district centres' cards do not.

The warning was in the files and did not change the night. By January the task force's corps groups held caches, couriers and committees that pointed at the towns around Tet. The combined estimate read them as local, and the leave order stood⁸.

The ARVN and the territorials go into Tet changed in four ways:
- every man carries a modern rifle;
- every man has passed the basic course;
- battalion commanders were chosen by the board;
- sergeants have been schooled.

In the district towns about a third of the attacks never get inside the compound walls. In IV and III Corps the battalions recall their men faster. The wounded of both allied armies are alive in larger numbers in the morning. At Cai Lay the posts that kept their listening posts out see the 514th Battalion coming and are left alone⁹¹⁰¹¹¹². In the cities the PAVN and the main force fight block by block, and there all of this lowers the cost without shortening the battles. Hue, fought under one combined commander, ends five days early¹³. The sappers who attack the combined headquarters carry a plan a traitor had drawn, and the compound holds.

When the government and CORDS move into the countryside after the offensives, they move into hamlets where about 900,000 hectares are already titled. Phoenix is only the name Washington learned for district centres that had run since 1964 without quotas and under an audit, and the Commission audits it against the land register⁵.

The mobilization of June finds rifles in stock, a training command that keeps the course at ten weeks, and platoon leaders who have passed the leader's course in about fourteen platoons in fifteen; its new units reach the field trained and a month late, and the academy and the sergeants' ranks pay for it¹⁰¹¹¹². The Front's third offensive goes for what no course reached, the People's Self-Defense Force, and COSVN works on the officers the board had passed over.

Above all this the radar watches the border. At Khe Sanh it measures the siege every night and its trenches are destroyed before they reach the wire; the PAVN pulls back about two weeks early at a much heavier price, and the garrison loses about a third fewer men. It is the most complete American victory of the war on the ground and changes nothing in Washington, and the brigade pulled from Thua Thien's hamlets to win it is missing when the Front returns to them. Abrams refuses to make it a doctrine of border bases and closes Khe Sanh on the historical date. After the halt the radar measures how the North uses it, and Commando Hunt opens against a panhandle net built to be cut, with a second ledger beside the Air Force's claims.

The President's decision of 31 March has no partial halt in it, because the campaign he had authorized in 1965 allowed none. Hanoi will not talk while the bombs fall, so the May and August offensives are fought with no table in Paris. The northern campaign goes on above the 19th parallel through the summer. It costs about 40 aircraft over the Hanoi and Haiphong gun belts, which history's campaign never risked¹⁴. The halt of 1 November comes on history's date and opens the talks themselves. The four-party conference meets in January, as it did historically: the six months lost in Paris were months history had spent on statements.

> 
> The private soldier in Tet is trained, and the mobilization of June finds a training base that will not send men to units untrained. In June the Joint General Staff wants the ten-week course cut to six to put the mobilization's men into the field by August; the training command holds it at ten by running the centres in two shifts, and the new battalions and territorial companies reach the field about a month later than history's and trained, with a man who has held the rank of sergeant in about four new PF platoons in five rather than two in three. >

The price is the academy's: its course is cut to four weeks for the duration, and its best instructors go to the new platoons.

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1968 the war has changed shape without changing direction. The VC in the South have lost much of their main and local forces and many of their cadres in the three offensives, and their recruitment has collapsed; the main-force war is now predominantly a PAVN war, and the parallel administration in the hamlets, though intact in much of the country, is under more pressure than at any time since 1959. The government in Saigon has survived Tet, mobilized, and begun with CORDS to push into the countryside; ARVN units fought better in February than anyone expected, though they remain dependent on American firepower and logistics. Against these gains, the United States has decided not to escalate further and to seek a negotiated way out; the bombing of the North has ended; and the American public's tolerance for casualties, measured in a year in which 14,592 Americans died by hostile action, has been spent³.

In Hanoi, the leadership has paid heavily for the General Offensive and turned back to protracted war for the moment, but has won what it most needed: an American president who will not reinforce and a successor committed to withdrawal. The Paris talks exist; the shape of the table is being settled. Phase IV opens with a new administration in Washington, a war in the countryside that the South is better placed to fight than it has been for years, and an American army whose withdrawal is now a matter of timing.

In this war the countryside is better placed than that, and the American decision of 1968 is unchanged, as is its timing.

- **The land.** About 900,000 hectares have been titled. The Front's Delta recruitment has fallen from a lower base, and its Delta battalions are filling with northerners earlier⁵.
- **The infrastructure.** In the held belt it is weaker than anywhere since 1959. The Tet losses fell on a network already broken there, and the Front's district committees enter 1969 governing from further out than history's.
- **The police.** The National Police numbers about 95,000, and every file it keeps is held under a destruction plan⁶.
- **Phung Hoang.** It enters 1969 with five years of files, an audited count the press has learned to quote, and no quotas. The Front's Delta committees have lost a third of the leaders they sent into the towns⁷. The Hue district files have shown what the national file would be worth to the enemy.
- **The combined command.** It found a traitor in its plans cell and has extended the two-layer plan to every corps. Hue was fought under one commander and ended five days early¹³.
- **The warning.** The files saw the towns' part of Tet and not its date⁸.

The RVNAF ends 1968 larger, with its battalions under commanders who held them through Tet and a board that has not stopped working¹⁰. It is armed throughout with weapons the historical army was still waiting for, a gap now closing from the historical side as the M16 reaches the ARVN in 1968 and the territorials in 1969⁹. The mobilization's soldiers are trained to the regulars' standard and reached the field about a month late¹¹. Its new platoons are led, in about fourteen cases in fifteen, by a man who passed the leader's course, against about two in three historically¹².

The mobilization's squads have no sergeants, its lieutenants were sergeants, and the academy's course is four weeks for the duration. The People's Self-Defense Force, which no course reached, has paid for the difference in Hau Nghia, Long An and Dinh Tuong. COSVN works among the officers the board passed over, and the Military Security Service keeps a second file on the board's officers, this time as targets.

About 2,150 rather than 2,788 ARVN soldiers died in the first wave. The hospitals of both armies are full of men who would have died on the historical course and are alive without a leg¹¹.

The PAVN leaves 1968 having learned that it does not lay siege to a position the Americans can measure. That is the one way of choosing its battles it has lost, and it chooses all the others¹⁵. The enemy's rear enters Phase IV counted. The surge after the halt is measured, and the first dry season of Commando Hunt is scored against the radar as well as the claims². The panhandle is harder to cut than history's, because the bombers taught its engineers how.

The northern campaign ends on 1 November, as history's did. It has lost about 810–880 aircraft rather than 922, and nothing is left in the North for it to destroy that the North could not rebuild in a night¹⁴. The talks that open on 13 November are the talks history opened in May, six months late and on the same terms, and Nixon inherits them on history's date.

The gap the rearmament opened over history is now closing from the historical side, as the M16 reaches the ARVN in 1968 and the territorials in 1969.
> 
> The PAVN leaves 1968 having learned that it does not lay siege to a position the Americans can measure; that is the one way of choosing its battles it has lost¹⁵. It chooses all the others. The panhandle is harder to cut than history's, because the bombers taught its engineers how.
> 
> Phung Hoang enters 1969 with five years of files, an audited count the press has learned to quote, and no quotas; the Front's Delta committees have lost a third of the leaders they sent into the towns⁷. The Hue district files have shown what the national file would be worth to the enemy. The selected advisers are in every field post, the first of them on their second tours, and the American battalions have fought the year as units.
> 
> The ARVN's battalions come out of 1968 with commanders who have held them through Tet and a board that has not stopped working; the mobilization's platoons have lieutenants who were sergeants and squads that have no sergeants¹⁰. COSVN has opened a campaign among the officers the board passed over, and the Military Security Service has a second file on the board's officers, this time as targets.
> 
> The RVNAF ends 1968 with the mobilization's soldiers trained to the same standard as the regulars of 1957, and about a month late in the field for it; the People's Self-Defense Force, which no course reached, has paid for the difference in Hau Nghia, Long An and Dinh Tuong. About 2,150 rather than 2,300 ARVN soldiers died in the first wave, and the hospitals of both armies are full of men who would have died on the historical course and are alive without a leg¹¹.
> 
> The RVNAF ends 1968 with its new platoons led, in about fourteen cases in fifteen, by a man who has passed the leader's course, against about four in five on the course of memorandum 009 and about two in three historically¹². The academy's course is four weeks for the duration and its field week intact. The posts of Cai Lay held Tet by not being attacked.
> 
> The combined command ends 1968 with a traitor found in its plans cell and the two-layer plan extended to every corps, and with one battle, Hue, fought under one commander and ended five days early¹³. The task force's work of 1965–67 showed at Tet on one road: the columns that came through Hoc Mon came through hamlets with no resident cadres to quarter or guide them. The infrastructure lost at Tet fell on a network already broken in the held belt, and the Front's district committees enter 1969 governing from further out than history's.
> 
> The northern campaign ends on 1 November as history's did, having lost about 810–880 aircraft rather than 922, and with nothing left in the North for it to destroy that the North could not rebuild in a night¹⁴. The talks that opened on 13 November are the talks history opened in May, six months late and on the same terms, and Nixon inherits them on history's date.

### Changed: The Tet Offensive: the first wave
*30–31 Jan 1968 · Saigon, Hue and the provincial and district capitals of South Vietnam · EV000-42*

*Initiative: enemy*
Shortly after midnight on 30 January, a day early because of a confusion in calendars, VC and PAVN forces attacked Nha Trang, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum, Hoi An, Tuy Hoa, Da Nang, Qui Nhon and Pleiku in I and II Corps. The warning was not fully heeded: half the ARVN was on holiday leave for Tet. At 03:00 on 31 January the main wave struck Saigon, Cholon and Gia Dinh and the rest of the country. In all, between about 70,000 and 84,000 PAVN and VC troops attacked more than 100 towns and cities: 36 of the 44 provincial capitals, 5 of the 6 autonomous cities, between 64 and 72 of the 245 district towns, and the capital⁴.

The plan called for the general offensive to set off a general uprising of the urban population. None came. In most towns the attackers were driven out within days by the ARVN, whose units, against American and Vietnamese expectations, generally fought, and by US forces; in Saigon, Hue, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum, Can Tho and Ben Tre the fighting lasted longer and destroyed large parts of the towns. The VC local forces and the urban cadres, who had surfaced to lead the uprising, were exposed and killed in large numbers. The United States claimed more than 45,000 PAVN and VC killed and 5,800 captured in the first phase, to 8 April, a figure even its own historians call excessively optimistic; Westmoreland gave 32,000 killed. Allied losses in the offensive were 2,788 ARVN killed, 8,299 wounded and 587 missing, and 1,536 US and other allied killed, 7,764 wounded and 11 missing. The PAVN official history gives communist casualties for the three phases of 1968 as 111,179, including 45,267 killed⁴.

In this war the first wave strikes the same towns on the same night, with the same forces⁵. The differences fall in IV and III Corps and in the district towns.

**The land and the police.** The battalions that attacked Can Tho and the Binh Thuy air base came up through the titled villages of Phong Dinh. GOLDEN SHEAF and the oil-spot of 1964–66 had left those villages in the hands of their own Popular Forces. PF platoons in at least six hamlets on the approaches reported the columns by AN/PRC-25 on the night of 30–31 January, and two of them fought. The 21st Division's reaction company and the Binh Thuy defenders were alerted about three hours before the assault⁵.

The attackers also waited for guides from two villages on the Xa No canal. The guides never arrived, because both villages had been taken in the night check two weeks earlier⁶. The attackers reached the university and the market but not the corps headquarters. Can Tho was cleared in about four days, by the 21st Division's battalions and the RF of Phong Dinh with VNAF A-1H support, and far less of the town was destroyed than on the historical course. Vinh Long, where titling had run along the river since 1964, was cleared in about three days⁵.

Ben Tre in Kien Hoa was the Front's oldest stronghold in the Delta. There the government had titled little outside the town, because it held little outside the town, and the battle and the destruction were as they were historically⁵. The difference ran exactly along the line of night security that the land programme had followed since 1964.

In Can Tho, My Tho and Vinh Long the Special Branch's urban sections had files on about a third of the legal cadres who surfaced to lead the uprising. In the first two weeks of February they arrested about 1,700 of them, on those files and on the identifications of constables and ward chiefs⁶. The infrastructure driven from the villages had gone to the towns.

The PIOCCs at Can Tho, My Tho and Vinh Long had carried charts of the province committees since 1965. The charts held photographs from the biometric enrolment of the cadres' arrested relatives and ralliers. About 140 province- and district-committee cadres came into the three towns to form the "revolutionary committees". About 50 of them were taken by 15 February, most on the identifications of ward police who had their photographs, and the Can Tho committee never held its first meeting⁷.

**The warning.** The checkpoint of memorandum 013 tested whether the files should have warned of Tet⁸. They held the pieces:
- the three Hoc Mon caches found in December from a courier's notebook;
- the province committees' preparations for the uprising in the Delta towns, which the district centres had been charting;
- the task force's national picture of the Front's political organisation.

What the files did not hold was the date or the scale. The order for the general offensive went down the military channels and reached the cadres in the towns only days before it, and the file saw the political half of the enemy, not the regiments⁸. The combined estimate of January 1968 read the pieces as preparations for attacks on the towns of the Delta and the Saigon belt around Tet, local in scale and secondary to Khe Sanh.

Two decisions above the level the files reached absorbed the warning, and they kept the national surprise:
- MACV judged the main effort to be in the north.
- The Joint General Staff's order that sent half the army on Tet leave stood until the first attacks in I and II Corps.

Below those decisions the warning showed. The III and IV Corps combined centres kept one reaction battalion in each divisional area at its towns over the holiday, and that is where the recall plans worked fastest⁸.

**The army in the towns.** By January 1968 about four in five ARVN battalion commanders had been chosen by the board and had held their battalions for more than a year. The board's commanders obeyed the leave order, but in IV and III Corps they had recall plans written to the career course's pattern¹⁰.

The 21st Division's desertion rate had fallen since the census reached its home districts in 1966. It stood at about 90 percent of its authorised strength on the muster roll⁶. Of that, by the evening of 31 January, the battalions of the 7th, 9th and 21st Divisions had about 70 percent in the towns against about half historically, a little more where the centres had held a battalion back¹⁰⁸.

Every ARVN soldier and territorial had carried a modern carbine for four years, and had passed the ten-week or the six-week course. The difference is clearest in the district towns. There the first wave was made by VC local-force battalions and companies against garrisons of an RF company or two, a PF platoon and the district police. I estimate that the attackers penetrated about two-thirds of the 64–72 district towns attacked, against nearly all historically⁹. The ones they did not enter were held by RF companies firing from their compound walls at men crossing open ground under flare light, as at Long Huu in 1964. The companies fired as the territorial course taught, in pairs, with ammunition kept for the second rush, under lieutenants many of whom had been sergeants in the same companies two years before¹⁰¹¹.

At Cai Lay on 31 January the 311th RF Company held the district compound until morning against a battalion of the 261st. It had one squad gun lent by the 7th Division and its own carbines. At 0600 it still had about a third of its basic load, and it was still firing at 0730, when the 2nd Battalion, 11th Regiment arrived. The battalion of the 261st had planned to be through the town by 0400⁹¹¹.

In Can Tho, Captain Jerome Pike, adviser to the 1st Battalion, 31st Regiment, took the call of a PF corporal on the Xa No canal in Vietnamese at 2340 on 30 January. He moved the battalion's reaction company to the university before the attackers reached it. The 9th Division's 2nd Brigade and the Mobile Riverine Force had been together since 1967, and they fought the streets of My Tho and Vinh Long as the units they had trained as⁷.

**The wounded.** Historically the ARVN's wounded in the offensive were about three times its dead⁴. In this war more of those torn by a B40 fragment or a burst of AK-47 fire were alive at dawn, because the man beside them had put on a tourniquet. In Hue the wounded of the 1st Division and the Marines lay in the Citadel's streets for a month, and the course saved men every day of it. The surgeons at Phu Bai complained, as Nha Trang's had in 1965, about tourniquets left on too long¹¹.

**The count.** Taking the rifles, the officers and the course together, I put the ARVN's killed in the first phase at about 2,150 against 2,788 historically⁹¹⁰. The rifles account for about 290 of the difference, the officers for about 200 and the course for about 150. I put the American killed in the first phase at about 30–60 fewer, at the rate shown at the Ia Drang¹¹. The warning in III and IV Corps does not move the count, because the dead fell at Saigon, Hue and the cities, where it changed nothing⁸. I do not adjust the enemy's losses, which were never measured to a precision these changes would show in.

None of this touched the outcome in Saigon, Hue or the Highlands, where the attackers were main-force units no district centre had charted⁶⁷. At Hue the 1st Division under Truong, the list's first name since 1966, fought as it fought historically.

### Changed: The battle of Hue
*31 Jan – 27 Feb 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · EV000-44*

*Initiative: enemy*
In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments with the 1st, 2nd and 12th Sapper Battalions, under a Hue City Front command, took almost all of Hue, the old imperial capital, except the ARVN 1st Division headquarters in the northeast corner of the Citadel and the MACV advisory compound south of the Perfume River. Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong held his headquarters with his staff and the Hac Bao Reconnaissance Company, and brought in the 3rd Regiment, the 4th Battalion, 2nd Regiment, the 1st Airborne Task Force (2nd and 7th Airborne Battalions), Vietnamese Marine Task Force A, the 7th Armored Cavalry Squadron and the 21st and 39th Ranger Battalions. The PAVN reinforced with the 7th Battalion, 29th Regiment of the 325C Division from Khe Sanh, the 803rd Regiment and a battalion of the 90th Regiment of the 324B Division, and the 6th Battalion, 24th Regiment of the 304th Division¹⁶.

South of the river the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines and the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 5th Marines of Task Force X-Ray cleared the new city block by block, house by house, in rain and low cloud that restricted air support for most of the battle. Outside the city the 3rd Brigade of the 1st Cavalry Division, with the 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry, the 5th Battalion, 7th Cavalry and the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry, fought to cut the PAVN routes in from the west; historically it did not reach the Citadel's west wall until 25 February¹⁶. Historically the ARVN and the Marines retook the Citadel, the flag of the Front came down from its tower on 24 February, and the battle was declared over on 2 March.

In this war Hue was one battle under one commander, and it ended about five days earlier. Historically it was three battles. Truong's division fought in the Citadel, the Marines fought south of the river under their own chain, and the 1st Cavalry Division's brigade fought to the west under the Army's, with no commander below Saigon over all three until MACV Forward was established at Phu Bai on 9 February. Here the I Corps combined centre at Da Nang, under Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam with Lieutenant General Robert E. Cushman of III Marine Amphibious Force as his deputy, named Truong commander of the battle of Hue at 1100 on 1 February. Brigadier General Foster C. LaHue of Task Force X-Ray became his deputy for the south bank, and the 3rd Brigade's commander became his deputy for the western approaches. One fire-support coordination centre in the Citadel took every call for naval gunfire, Marine and Army artillery and the aircraft the weather allowed, from Vietnamese and American units alike, through the switchboard the combined command had run in I Corps since 1966¹³.

The change that shortened the battle was in the west. Truong's first request to the combined centre, on the afternoon of 1 February, was for the western routes to be cut before anything else, because the PAVN was reinforcing through La Chu and the hamlets of Thon Que Chu. It was the reinforcement, not the walls, that would make the Citadel long. The combined centre gave the 3rd Brigade first call on the I Corps helicopter lift from 2 February and placed the ARVN 1st Division's 3rd Regiment under the brigade's command for the block. Historically the brigade was short of lift and fought its way overland from PK-17. The brigade reached the Citadel's west wall on 20 February rather than 25 February. The 803rd Regiment's battalion from the 324B Division, which historically entered the city through La Chu in mid-February, was caught in the open at Thon La Chu on 12–13 February by the brigade and the ARVN 3rd Regiment together, with naval gunfire from the cruiser and destroyers of the gunfire support group off the coast, called through the Citadel's centre, and broken. The flag of the Front came down from the Citadel tower on 19 February, and the combined command declared the battle over on 27 February¹³. The weather and the walls still set most of the battle's length, and nothing in the combined command touched either.

The squad weapons made Hue somewhat less costly to retake and no shorter. On the first night the Hac Bao company held the 1st Division compound with M4A1s and four squad guns against the 800th and 802nd Battalions' assault teams. The difference was small, because the Hac Bao was among the few ARVN units historically re-armed by then. Across the river the Marines had two or three M249s in each squad and a marksman with an M110A2, who could put rounds into an upper-floor window at 200 metres from cover. The 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines credited its marksmen with most of the PAVN machine gunners killed on the treasury and the public health building between 4 and 6 February. What took the blocks was what took them historically: the 106mm recoilless rifles, the Ontos, tear gas and men going through walls. Against 458 ARVN and 250 American dead historically, the rifles alone would have made them about 410 and 215⁹. With the battle about five days shorter and the western reinforcement broken at La Chu, I put them at about 370 and 200, and the destruction a little less in the Citadel's western quarter, which was the last to be cleared¹³.

The ARVN lost 458 killed and about 2,700 wounded, and the Americans 250 killed and 1,554 wounded, on the historical course. PAVN and VC dead are given from 1,042 to more than 5,000, by source. Between 5,800 and 8,000 civilians died and the city was largely destroyed. During their occupation the PAVN and VC rounded up officials, officers, priests, teachers, foreigners and others on prepared lists; after the battle mass graves were found, and more than 2,000 people are known to have been executed, with the most cited count of bodies recovered at about 2,800¹⁶. Hue was the only city the offensive held for more than a few days, and the killings there hardened the urban population of the South against the Front for the rest of the war. The five days the combined command saved were not days on which the security sections' killing stopped. Most of the executions were carried out in the first two weeks, and the shorter battle saved, I judge, a few hundred of the city's civilian dead at most, from the shelling of the western quarter rather than from the lists¹³.

In this war the battle is the same battle, and the killings are worse in one particular. The Front's Hue city security section drew its lists in this war from three sources it did not have on the historical course: a copy of the Hue family census taken from the provincial identity office through an agent in its records room in 1967, the knowledge of the Struggle Movement's student leaders who had gone to the Front after the repression of 1966, and the names of the constables and Special Branch officers of Thua Thien, which the census itself recorded by household. The teams that went through Phu Cam, Gia Hoi and the streets around the Citadel in February went to houses, not to neighbourhoods. Of the dead identified in the graves found in 1968–69, police officers, constables, census clerks and their families were about a fifth on this course, against a smaller share on the historical one. I do not raise the total. I cannot show that more people were killed, only that the lists were better and the choice of whom to kill more exact; the Mission's count of the dead is the historical count, and it is a floor⁶.

The consequence was immediate in the Directorate. On 9 March 1968 Loan's deputy issued the order this headquarters had urged in 1964 and the Directorate had deferred. Every district and province office was to hold its census copies, informant cards and Special Branch files under a destruction plan, with thermite charges and a quarterly rehearsal⁶. The order was written with the Huong Thuy file in front of it.

The Thua Thien province centre was in the province headquarters south of the river, which the attackers held until the 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines retook it on 6 February¹⁶. Its informant cards never reached the attackers. Against Hieu's rule, the PIOCC's chief, Major Ton That Dinh Lang, had kept the cards of the province's 340 informants in a single safe, because he did not trust his district centres' security. When the attack reached the compound wall at about 0330 on 31 January, he burned the cards in the safe with a can of gasoline. He was killed an hour later on the stairs⁷.

The district centres of Huong Thuy and Phu Vang, outside the city, kept their copies and lost them when their offices were overrun on 31 January and 1 February. The security section's lists for the southern suburbs included about 60 informants and centre staff named from those files. About 40 of them were among the dead found in the graves at Phu Thu and Da Mai Creek⁷. The national file in Saigon held every one of those names and was never in danger in 1968. It was the first time the record showed what a fused file was worth to the enemy.

> 
> South of the river the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines and the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 5th Marines of Task Force X-Ray cleared the new city block by block, house by house, in rain and low cloud that restricted air support for most of the battle. Outside the city the 3rd Brigade of the 1st Cavalry Division, with the 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry, the 5th Battalion, 7th Cavalry and the 2nd Battalion, 501st Infantry, fought to cut the PAVN routes in from the west; historically it did not reach the Citadel's west wall until 25 February. Historically the ARVN and the Marines retook the Citadel, the flag of the Front came down from its tower on 24 February, and the battle was declared over on 2 March.
> 
> In this war Hue was one battle under one commander, and it ended about five days earlier. Historically it was three battles. Truong's division fought in the Citadel, the Marines fought south of the river under their own chain, and the 1st Cavalry Division's brigade fought to the west under the Army's, with no commander below Saigon over all three until MACV Forward was established at Phu Bai on 9 February. Here the I Corps combined centre at Da Nang, under Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam with Lieutenant General Robert E. Cushman of III Marine Amphibious Force as his deputy, named Truong commander of the battle of Hue at 1100 on 1 February. Brigadier General Foster C. LaHue of Task Force X-Ray became his deputy for the south bank, and the 3rd Brigade's commander became his deputy for the western approaches. One fire-support coordination centre in the Citadel took every call for naval gunfire, Marine and Army artillery and the aircraft the weather allowed, from Vietnamese and American units alike, through the switchboard the combined command had run in I Corps since 1966.
> 
> The change that shortened the battle was in the west. Truong's first request to the combined centre, on the afternoon of 1 February, was for the western routes to be cut before anything else, because the PAVN was reinforcing through La Chu and the hamlets of Thon Que Chu. It was the reinforcement, not the walls, that would make the Citadel long. The combined centre gave the 3rd Brigade first call on the I Corps helicopter lift from 2 February and placed the ARVN 1st Division's 3rd Regiment under the brigade's command for the block. Historically the brigade was short of lift and fought its way overland from PK-17. The brigade reached the Citadel's west wall on 20 February rather than 25 February. The 803rd Regiment's battalion from the 324B Division, which historically entered the city through La Chu in mid-February, was caught in the open at Thon La Chu on 12–13 February by the brigade and the ARVN 3rd Regiment together, with naval gunfire from the cruiser and destroyers of the gunfire support group off the coast, called through the Citadel's centre, and broken. The flag of the Front came down from the Citadel tower on 19 February, and the combined command declared the battle over on 27 February. The weather and the walls still set most of the battle's length, and nothing in the combined command touched either.
> 
> The squad weapons made Hue somewhat less costly to retake and no shorter. On the first night the Hac Bao company held the 1st Division compound with M4A1s and four squad guns against the 800th and 802nd Battalions' assault teams, where historically it held with M16s it had only recently received; the difference was small, because the Hac Bao was among the few ARVN units historically re-armed by then. Across the river the Marines fought the street battle with two or three M249s in each squad and a marksman with an M110A2 who, in a city where the PAVN held the upper floors and the far side of every street, could put rounds into a window at 200 metres from cover that a squad's rifles could not reach. The 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines' after-action report credited its marksmen with most of the PAVN machine gunners killed on the treasury and the public health building between 4 and 6 February. What took the blocks was what took them historically: the 106mm recoilless rifles, the Ontos, tear gas and men going through walls. The weather, the Citadel's walls and the PAVN's reinforcement from the west set the length of the battle, and the rifles touched none of them. I put the ARVN dead at about 410 and the American at about 215, against 458 and 250 historically⁹. With the battle about five days shorter and the western reinforcement broken at La Chu, I put them at about 370 and 200 in this war, and the city's destruction a little less in the Citadel's western quarter, which was the last to be cleared.
> 
> The ARVN lost 458 killed and about 2,700 wounded, and the Americans 250 killed and 1,554 wounded, on the historical course. PAVN and VC dead are given from 1,042 to more than 5,000, by source. Between 5,800 and 8,000 civilians died and the city was largely destroyed. During their occupation the PAVN and VC rounded up officials, officers, priests, teachers, foreigners and others on prepared lists; after the battle mass graves were found, and more than 2,000 people are known to have been executed, with the most cited count of bodies recovered at about 2,800. Hue was the only city the offensive held for more than a few days, and the killings there hardened the urban population of the South against the Front for the rest of the war. The five days the combined command saved were not days on which the security sections' killing stopped. Most of the executions were carried out in the first two weeks, and the shorter battle saved, I judge, a few hundred of the city's civilian dead at most, from the shelling of the western quarter rather than from the lists¹³.
> 
> In this war the battle is the same battle, and the killings are worse in one particular. The Front's Hue city security section drew its lists in this war from three sources it did not have on the historical course: a copy of the Hue family census taken from the provincial identity office through an agent in its records room in 1967, the knowledge of the Struggle Movement's student leaders who had gone to the Front after the repression of 1966, and the names of the constables and Special Branch officers of Thua Thien, which the census itself recorded by household. The teams that went through Phu Cam, Gia Hoi and the streets around the Citadel in February went to houses, not to neighbourhoods. Of the dead identified in the graves found in 1968–69, police officers, constables, census clerks and their families were about a fifth on this course, against a smaller share on the historical one. I do not raise the total. I cannot show that more people were killed, only that the lists were better and the choice of whom to kill more exact; the Mission's count of the dead is the historical count, and it is a floor.
> 
> The consequence was immediate in the Directorate. On 9 March 1968 Loan's deputy issued the order that this headquarters had urged in 1964 and the Directorate had deferred: every district and province office was to hold its census copies, informant cards and Special Branch files under a destruction plan, with thermite charges and a rehearsal every quarter⁶. In the provinces the plan was rehearsed. Whether it would be carried out on the day it was needed was a question for another year.
> 
> The Thua Thien province centre was in the province headquarters south of the river, which the attackers held from 31 January until the 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines retook it on 6 February¹⁶. Its informant cards were not in the attackers' hands. The PIOCC's chief, Major Ton That Dinh Lang, had kept the cards of the province's 340 informants in a single safe, against Hieu's rule, because he did not trust his district centres' security; when the attack reached the compound wall at about 0330 on 31 January he burned the cards in the safe with a can of gasoline and was killed an hour later on the stairs. The district centres of Huong Thuy and Phu Vang, outside the city, kept their copies and lost them when their offices were overrun on 31 January and 1 February; the Hue city security section's lists for the southern suburbs included about 60 informants and centre staff named from those files, of whom about 40 were among the dead found in the graves at Phu Thu and Da Mai Creek⁷. The national file in Saigon, which held every one of those names, was never in danger in 1968. It was the first time the record showed what a fused file was worth to the enemy, and the destruction order of 9 March was written with the Huong Thuy file in front of it.

### New: The May fighting: Dai Do, the second wave in Saigon and Kham Duc
*30 Apr – 15 Jun 1968 · Dai Do and the hamlets north of Dong Ha, Quang Tri Province; Saigon, Cholon and towns throughout the South; Kham Duc and Ngok Tavak, Quang Tin Province · EVCP03-1*

*Initiative: enemy*

These three battles are told together because they showed one thing three ways. Hanoi kept the offensive going after February at a price it chose to pay, and none of the provisions reached the places it chose.

**Dai Do.** At the end of April, as the second wave began, battalions of the PAVN 320th Division moved into the hamlets of Dai Do, Dinh To and their neighbours north of Dong Ha, threatening the Marine base and the Cua Viet supply route. Two of the battalions were identified as belonging to the 48th and 52nd Regiments. The 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines under Lieutenant Colonel William Weise attacked across open paddies from amphibian tractors and boats. With it were the 1st Battalion, 3rd Marines, ARVN units of the 2nd Regiment and a mechanized battalion, and from 1 May the US 3rd Battalion, 21st Infantry. The Marines lost 81 killed and the ARVN 5. The Americans claimed more than 600 PAVN killed; the PAVN has not released its losses. By 3 May the PAVN had gone. Whether Dai Do was a main thrust or a diversion is not settled¹⁷.

**Saigon.** On 5 May the PAVN and VC launched the second phase of the general offensive, which the Americans called "mini-Tet". It began with attacks by fire on more than 100 towns and installations and a renewed assault on Saigon. VC battalions fought into the southern and western districts and Cholon. They were destroyed or driven out over several weeks, with air strikes and artillery used inside the city. Much of District 8 was destroyed and tens of thousands were made homeless. The phase lasted until 15 June⁴. Its losses fell on the local forces and cadres who had survived February, and many units were filled out with northern replacements. American deaths in May 1968 were the highest of any month of the war.

**Kham Duc.** On 10 May the 40th Battalion of the PAVN 2nd Division's 1st Regiment overran Ngok Tavak, held by an Australian-led company of the 11th MIKE Force and a battery of the 2nd Battalion, 13th Marines. The 1st and 21st Regiments then closed on Kham Duc, held by Detachment A-105, CIDG, a SOG detachment and the 2nd Battalion, 1st Infantry. On 12 May, under about 350 air sorties, roughly 1,500 soldiers and civilians were flown out. A C-130 flown by Major Bernard L. Bucher was shot down after take-off, killing all 183 Vietnamese civilians aboard, a Special Forces officer and the five crewmen. Lieutenant Colonel Joe M. Jackson landed a C-123 on the abandoned strip to recover a three-man combat control team, and received the Medal of Honor. The Americans lost about 42–46 killed, 31–33 missing and twelve aircraft. About 220 CIDG were killed or missing. The US claimed about 345 PAVN killed, and a later study estimates 1,500–2,000. Kham Duc was one of the few clear PAVN victories over a US-defended position in 1968¹⁸.

**In this war.** All three run as they did historically, and what absorbs the record's changes is the enemy's choice of ground⁸:
- Dai Do and Kham Duc lie in I Corps outside the titled and policed belt.
- The May assault on Saigon came from the south and west, through Cholon and District 8, not through the Hoc Mon corridor the task force had emptied.
- In May, as in February, the attackers were main-force units that no district centre charted.

The ARVN's share of Saigon's fighting is smaller in losses by the same rule as February's, which I do not count again.

### No longer happens: The battle of Dai Do
*30 Apr – 3 May 1968 · Dai Do and the hamlets north of Dong Ha on the Cua Viet, Quang Tri Province · EV000-47*

*Consolidated at CP03 into EVCP03-1; the event still happens.*

**Before:**

> At the end of April, as the second wave of the offensive began, battalions of the PAVN 320th Division, two of them identified as belonging to the 48th and 52nd Regiments, moved into the hamlets of Dai Do, Dinh To and their neighbours north of Dong Ha, threatening the Marine base and the Cua Viet supply route. The 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines under Lieutenant Colonel William Weise attacked across open paddies from amphibian tractors and boats, with the 1st Battalion, 3rd Marines, ARVN units of the 2nd Regiment and a mechanized battalion, and from 1 May the US 3rd Battalion, 21st Infantry. The Marines lost 81 killed and the ARVN 5; the Americans claimed more than 600 PAVN killed, and the PAVN has not released its losses. By 3 May the PAVN had gone. Whether Dai Do was a main thrust against Dong Ha or a diversion is not settled; the frontal assaults of 1 and 2 May were costly enough to be criticized by later historians¹⁷.

### No longer happens: The May offensive in Saigon
*5 May – 15 Jun 1968 · Saigon and its outskirts, and towns throughout the South · EV000-49*

*Consolidated at CP03 into EVCP03-1; the event still happens.*

**Before:**

> On 5 May the PAVN and VC launched the second phase of the general offensive, which the Americans called "mini-Tet", with attacks by fire on more than 100 towns and installations and a renewed assault on Saigon. VC battalions fought their way into the southern and western districts of the capital and into Cholon, where they were destroyed or driven out by the ARVN and US forces over several weeks, with air strikes and artillery used inside the city; much of District 8 was destroyed and tens of thousands were made homeless. The phase lasted until 15 June⁴. Its losses fell heavily on the same local forces and cadres who had survived February, and many of the units that fought in Saigon in May were filled out with northern replacements. American deaths in May 1968 were the highest of any month of the war.

### No longer happens: The evacuation of Kham Duc
*10–12 May 1968 · Kham Duc Special Forces camp and Ngok Tavak, Quang Tin Province · EV000-50*

*Consolidated at CP03 into EVCP03-1; the event still happens.*

**Before:**

> On 10 May the 40th Battalion of the PAVN 2nd Division's 1st Regiment overran the outpost of Ngok Tavak, held by an Australian-led company of the 11th MIKE Force and a battery of the 2nd Battalion, 13th Marines. The PAVN 1st and 21st Regiments then closed on the camp at Kham Duc, held by Special Forces Detachment A-105, CIDG and a SOG detachment, reinforced by the 2nd Battalion, 1st Infantry of the Americal Division. On 11 May Westmoreland approved evacuation, and on 12 May, under about 350 air sorties, roughly 1,500 soldiers and civilians were flown out. A C-130 flown by Major Bernard L. Bucher was shot down just after take-off, killing all 183 Vietnamese civilians aboard, a Special Forces officer and the five crewmen; a second C-130 was wrecked on the runway. Lieutenant Colonel Joe M. Jackson landed a C-123 on the abandoned strip to recover a three-man combat control team left behind, and received the Medal of Honor. The Americans lost about 42–46 killed and 31–33 missing and twelve aircraft; about 220 CIDG were killed or missing; the US claimed about 345 PAVN killed, and a later study estimates 1,500–2,000. The abandonment of the camp removed one of the few allied positions between the Laotian border and the lowlands of Quang Tin and Quang Nam, and its loss was one of the few clear PAVN victories over a US-defended position in 1968¹⁸.

### Changed: Abrams takes command; mobilization in the South; Khe Sanh abandoned
*10 Jun – 11 Jul 1968 · Saigon and Quang Tri Province · EV000-51*

*Initiative: allied*

On 10 June 1968 General Creighton W. Abrams, Westmoreland's deputy since May 1967, succeeded him as COMUSMACV; Westmoreland went home to be Army Chief of Staff. Abrams spoke of "one war", in which the main-force battle, pacification and the improvement of the RVNAF were parts of one campaign rather than separate efforts, and gave more weight to the enemy's logistics system, to territorial security and to the South Vietnamese forces. How much changed in practice is disputed: large operations continued into 1969 and his own strategy papers did not announce a new strategy¹⁹.

In mid-June the National Assembly in Saigon passed the general mobilization law the government had been unable to pass before Tet, inducting men aged 18 to 38 and ordering youths of 17 and men of 39 to 43 into civil defence; about 220,000 men were inducted before the summer ended. RVNAF strength rose from about 643,000 in 1967 to about 897,000 in 1969²⁰. Historically the expansion outran the rifles. The M16 went first to the regular divisions in 1968, and the Regional and Popular Forces raised that summer drew carbines and Garands and waited until 1969–70 for anything better.

In this war the new RF companies and PF platoons drew M4A1s from the 1968 increment. About 260,000 carbines were already in the depots at Long Binh and Da Nang by June, against the year's expected growth. The old weapons went, with the Garands the Combat Youth already held, to the People's Self-Defense Force formed under the same law. Its members got a few days of instruction from the district chiefs, as historically, because no course reached them⁹.

The constraint on the expansion was not rifles but leaders, and three reforms met it in turn; the figures below are the record's net result.

**Officers.** Historically the Thu Duc candidate course was cut from 37 weeks to 24 in June 1968²¹. In this war it was cut to 32 weeks, and the field commissions filled the gap. About 3,000 sergeants had been commissioned since 1966, and about 2,500 more were commissioned in the second half of 1968 after the branch basic course. The board's lists governed the new RF companies from their first month, and the new PF platoons not at all. The price fell on the ranks the lieutenants came from: by the end of 1968 the army had made lieutenants of about 5,500 of its best sergeants¹⁰.

**Training.** Historically the RVNAF sent some draftees to units untrained, and the basic course was cut from twelve weeks to nine. In this war the Joint General Staff ordered the course cut to six weeks on 21 June. The Central Training Command, with Coyle's successor and the Muster Service's chief behind it, answered that six weeks would leave out the Forge and the field week. It proposed instead to run the 33 national and division centres in two daily shifts, which raised their capacity from about 65,000 to about 105,000 in cycle²². The Joint General Staff accepted on 28 June. About 40,000 of the 220,000 inductees waited three to six weeks for a cycle to open. The new battalions and territorial companies reached the field trained, about a month later than history's, in September and October and after the third offensive had begun¹¹.

**Sergeants and corporals.** On the historical training base the field commissions would have left about a third of the new PF platoons with no one who had held the rank of sergeant⁹. In this war the drill-sergeant corps had returned about 650–1,800 sergeants a year to the battalions since 1966, and in July 1968 the training command released about 1,100 more from the second shift to the new platoons. That cut the share without a sergeant to about a fifth¹¹. Where no sergeant could be found, the platoon was given a corporal first class who had passed the leader's course and served a year in an RF company. In 1968 about two in three corporals first class in the regular battalions, and about half in the RF companies, had passed it. About two in three of the platoons without a sergeant got such a man. Venn's successor reported in September that about one new PF platoon in fifteen had no leader who had passed the course¹².

The academy paid. The Joint General Staff ordered the leader's course cut to three weeks. The training command kept the field week and cut the classroom, and the course ran at four weeks from July 1968 to June 1969, its second shift taught by instructors who had been platoon sergeants in 1967¹².

On Khe Sanh the decision was harder than it had been historically, because in this war the base had been a victory rather than an ordeal. Westmoreland, in his last weeks, argued for keeping it as the anchor of a line of border bases under the siege box, and the III Marine Amphibious Force's staff drew up a plan for three more such bases along Route 9 and the Laotian border, to be held by battalions drawn from the coastal districts. Abrams refused it on 15 June. His reason, in a message to Wheeler that his staff kept, was that a base the enemy would not attack was a base that held nothing, and that after Khe Sanh the enemy would not attack one. On 19 June the Marines began evacuating Khe Sanh; the base was closed on 5 July and the last Marines left the area on 11 July²³. The decision was explained as the product of more helicopters and a mobile defence of the DMZ. Here it was read in Hanoi correctly, as a decision by an American commander that the siege the PAVN had lost was not worth inviting again, and in the American press, less correctly, as a retreat from a battle won¹⁵.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> On 10 June 1968 General Creighton W. Abrams, Westmoreland's deputy since May 1967, succeeded him as COMUSMACV; Westmoreland went home to be Army Chief of Staff. Abrams spoke of "one war", in which the main-force battle, pacification and the improvement of the RVNAF were parts of one campaign rather than separate efforts, and gave more weight to the enemy's logistics system, to territorial security and to the South Vietnamese forces. How much changed in practice is disputed: large operations continued into 1969 and his own strategy papers did not announce a new strategy¹⁹.
>

RVNAF strength rose from about 643,000 in 1967 to about 897,000 in 1969²⁰. Historically the expansion outran the rifles: the M16 went first to the regular divisions in 1968, and the Regional and Popular Forces raised that summer drew carbines and Garands and waited until 1969–70 for anything better. In this war the new RF companies and PF platoons drew M4A1s from the 1968 increment, about 260,000 carbines already in the depots at Long Binh and Da Nang by June against the year's expected growth, and were on the ranges within a month of induction. The constraint on the expansion was not rifles but sergeants: the training centres could zero a carbine in an afternoon and could not make a squad leader in less than a year, and Venn's successor reported in September that about a third of the new PF platoons had no one who had held the rank before. The old weapons the RVNAF had handed in since 1964 went, with the Garands the Combat Youth already held, to the People's Self-Defense Force formed under the same law⁹.
> 
> On Khe Sanh the decision was harder than it had been historically, because in this war the base had been a victory rather than an ordeal. Westmoreland, in his last weeks, argued for keeping it as the anchor of a line of border bases under the siege box, and the III Marine Amphibious Force's staff drew up a plan for three more such bases along Route 9 and the Laotian border, to be held by battalions drawn from the coastal districts. Abrams refused it on 15 June. His reason, in a message to Wheeler that his staff kept, was that a base the enemy would not attack was a base that held nothing, and that after Khe Sanh the enemy would not attack one. On 19 June the Marines began evacuating Khe Sanh; the base was closed on 5 July and the last Marines left the area on 11 July²³. The decision was explained as the product of more helicopters and a mobile defence of the DMZ. Here it was read in Hanoi correctly, as a decision by an American commander that the siege the PAVN had lost was not worth inviting again, and in the American press, less correctly, as a retreat from a battle won¹⁵.
> 
> The officers for the mobilization came differently. Historically the Thu Duc candidate course was cut from 37 weeks to 24 in June 1968 to commission the platoon leaders the expansion needed²¹. In this war the cut was to 32 weeks, and the gap was filled by the field commissions: about 3,000 sergeants had been commissioned since 1966 and about 2,500 more were commissioned in the second half of 1968, after the branch basic course that the decree did not allow to be waived. The cost was in the ranks they came from. The sergeant shortage that Venn's successor reported in September, a third of the new PF platoons with no one who had held the rank, was in part the field commission's price: the army had made lieutenants of the sergeants who would have led those platoons¹⁰. The board's lists governed the new RF companies from their first month, and the new PF platoons not at all.
> 
> The mobilization met a training base that would not send men to units untrained, and the cost was a month. Historically the RVNAF in 1968 sent some draftees straight to units without basic training, and the ARVN basic course was cut from twelve weeks to nine to put men through faster. In this war, on 21 June, the Joint General Staff ordered the course cut to six weeks for the duration of the mobilization; the Central Training Command, with Coyle's successor and the Muster Service's chief behind it, answered that six weeks would leave out the Forge and the field week, the part the new soldier most needed, and proposed instead to run the 33 national and division centres in two daily shifts, which raised their capacity from about 65,000 to about 105,000 in cycle²². The Joint General Staff accepted on 28 June. About 220,000 men were inducted before the summer ended; about 40,000 of them waited three to six weeks at the centres for a cycle to open, and the new battalions and territorial companies reached the field about a month later than they did historically, after the third offensive had begun rather than before it. They reached it trained. The new RF companies and PF platoons of the summer went through the six-week territorial course as platoons, on the M4A1 they had drawn from the depots, and came back to their districts in September and October rather than August.
> 
> The sergeants came differently too, and the result was not the one memorandum 007 predicted. The field commissions had made lieutenants of about 5,500 of the army's best sergeants by the end of 1968, and on the historical training base that would have left the new PF platoons with no one who had held the rank. In this war the drill-sergeant corps had been returning sergeants to the battalions since 1966, about 650–1,800 a year, and in July 1968 the training command released about 1,100 more from the centres' second shift to the new territorial platoons, each a man who had trained a platoon of recruits for two years. Venn's successor reported in September that about a fifth of the new PF platoons had no one who had held the rank of sergeant, rather than about a third¹¹. The People's Self-Defense Force, which the law raised in the same summer and which the course did not reach, was given its Garands and carbines and a few days of instruction by the district chiefs, as historically.
> 
> The schooled corporal filled what was left. The leader's course had been taught to corporals first class since 1957, regular and territorial, and in 1968 about two in three of the corporals first class in the regular battalions and about half of those in the RF companies had passed it. The training command gave the new PF platoons their leaders from that pool: where no sergeant could be found, the platoon was given a corporal first class who had passed the course and had served a year in an RF company, as acting platoon leader. Of the fifth of new platoons with no one who had held the rank of sergeant, about two in three got such a man, and Venn's successor reported in September that about one PF platoon in fifteen had no leader who had passed the course. The academy paid. The Joint General Staff ordered the leader's course cut to three weeks for the mobilization; the training command, on the precedent of the basic course, kept the field week and cut the classroom, and the course ran at four weeks from July 1968 to June 1969, with the academy's second shift taught by instructors who had been platoon sergeants in 1967¹². In the regular battalions, about two in three of the squads the commissions had emptied were held by acting leaders who had passed the course.
